deep.reconstruction:
This is a printed page, p. 54 of Leiste's arithmetic/algebra textbook from Gauss's copy, with Gauss's handwritten notes in the right margin.

PRINTED TEXT

(a) Conclusion of the inverse rule-of-three example from p. 53. A length C is measured with two units B and A, where B:A = 3:2, and C = 4B. Then
  C/3 : C/2 = 2C/6 : 3C/6 = 2:3 (§128) = 4 (ells of B) : x,
  so x = 3·4/2 = 6 ells of A.
The point is that the number of units is inversely proportional to the unit size. The book handles this by writing the reciprocal fractions C/3 and C/2.

(b) Brabant ell : Leipzig ell = 6:5. How many Leipzig ells are 25 Brabant ells? With C the length,
  C/6 : C/5 = 5:6 = 25 : 30,
so the answer is 30 Leipzig ells.

(c) §131, Lehrsatz (componendo/dividendo). If a:b = p:q, then
  (a+b):a = (p+q):p,
  (a+b):b = (p+q):q,
  (a−b):a = (p−q):p,
  (a−b):b = (p−q):q.
Proof. From aq = bp:
  1) add ap to both sides: ap+aq = ap+bp, i.e. (a+b)p = (p+q)a;
  2) subtract from ap: ap−aq = ap−bp, i.e. (a−b)p = (p−q)a;
  3) add bq: aq+bq = bp+bq, i.e. (a+b)q = (p+q)b;
  4) subtract bq: aq−bq = bp−bq, i.e. (a−b)q = (p−q)b.
By §125 (product of means equals product of extremes, and conversely) these give the stated proportions.

(d) §132. If a:b:c = p:q:r, then aq = bp, br = cq and ar = cp. Hence
  ap+bp+cp = ap+aq+ar, i.e. (a+b+c)p = (p+q+r)a,
so (a+b+c):a = (p+q+r):p. Similarly for b and c.

Application (proportional division, 'Gesellschaftsrechnung'): given n = p+q+r and the ratio a:b:c,
  p = an/(a+b+c), q = bn/(a+b+c), r = cn/(a+b+c).
So one computes the factor n/(a+b+c) once and multiplies it by a, b and c in turn. The same works for more parts.

GAUSS'S MARGINALIA (fragmentary; continued on the next page)

(i) Rational approximations to π: 3 17/120 = 3.141666… and 3 785/5544 = 3.1415945…, plus a fraction read as 99/40 (uncertain). On the next page he decomposes these into sums of fractions.

(ii) The start of '1/√(1+sin…', 'a =', '= ∫√…', 'b ='. This is the beginning of the next page's 'Bestimmung der zwei ersten Coefficienten' of
  1/√(1+sin²φ) = a + b cos2φ − c cos4φ − …
There
  a = Σ_k (−1)^k [(2k)!/(4^k k!²)]² = 1/AGM(1,√2) = (2/π)∫_0^1 dx/√(1−x⁴) = 0.83462…
This is Gauss's lemniscatic constant. The next page also has b = 2a − 2/A (his notation).

Only the stubs of (ii) are on this page.
errors: No arithmetic errors in the printed text: 6 ells and 30 Leipzig ells are both correct.

§131: the proof tacitly assumes the terms a, p (resp. b, q) are nonzero. For the difference forms it also tacitly assumes a≠b, p≠q, or at least avoids division by zero when the proportions are interpreted as quotients. This is standard textbook looseness.
§132: the book only writes out the derivation (a+b+c)p = (p+q+r)a using equations 1) and 3). Equation 2) br = cq is used only for the 'similarly' cases. This is fine.

deep.surprise_reason: The printed text is routine 18th-century textbook arithmetic. The margin notes are fragmentary starts of Gauss's well-known lemniscate/AGM work (constant 0.83462…), which is documented in his diary and Nachlass. Notes in his copy of Leiste are already known to Gauss scholarship, so nothing here is new.
